claim: The Gastric Mill (GM) neuron in the crustacean stomatogastric ganglion (STG) operates like a single electrotonic compartment, despite having thousands of branch points and total cable length >10 mm.
source: previously we showed that the Gastric Mill (GM) neuron in the crustacean stomatogastric ganglion (STG) operates like a single electrotonic compartment, despite having thousands of branch points and total cable length >10 mm (Otopalik et al., 2017a; 2017b)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work (Otopalik et al., 2017a; 2017b) that demonstrated this finding.

claim: Compact electrotonic architecture is generalizable to other STG neuron types beyond the GM neuron.
source: Here we show that compact electrotonic architecture is generalizable to other STG neuron types
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript showing measurements across multiple STG neuron types (PD, LP, VD, GM).

claim: STG neurons present direction-insensitive, linear voltage integration.
source: these neurons present direction-insensitive, linear voltage integration, suggesting they pool synaptic inputs across their neuronal structures
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from glutamate photo-uncaging experiments shown in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: STG neurons pool synaptic inputs across their neuronal structures.
source: these neurons present direction-insensitive, linear voltage integration, suggesting they pool synaptic inputs across their neuronal structures
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observed direction-insensitive, linear voltage integration properties.

claim: Compact electrotonus, linear integration, and directional insensitivity in STG neurons arise from their neurite geometries (diameters tapering from 10-20 µm to < 2 µm at their terminal tips).
source: compact electrotonus, linear integration, and directional insensitivity in STG neurons arise from their neurite geometries (diameters tapering from 10-20 µm to < 2 µm at their terminal tips)
evidence: This claim is supported by computational simulations of 720 cable models and experimental measurements of neurite geometries.

claim: Multiple morphological and biophysical solutions exist for achieving different degrees of passive electrotonic decrement and computational strategies in the absence of active properties.
source: A broad parameter search reveals multiple morphological and biophysical solutions for achieving different degrees of passive electrotonic decrement and computational strategies in the absence of active properties.
evidence: This claim is supported by computational simulations exploring a broad parameter space of cable models with varying geometries and passive properties.

claim: Passive voltage propagation is influenced by the neurite's diameter, membrane resistance, and axial resistance.
source: Passive voltage propagation is influenced by the neurite's diameter, membrane resistance, and axial resistance (Rall, 1959; Rall, 1960; Rall, 1969; Jack et al., 1975; Holmes, 1989)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to foundational theoretical work in cable theory.

claim: Rall and colleagues were the first to apply passive cable theory and develop the equivalent cylinder model for the study of electrotonus in single dendrites and branched dendritic trees.
source: Rall and colleages were the first to apply passive cable theory and develop the equivalent cylinder model for the study of electrotonus in single dendrites and branched dendritic trees (Rall, 1959; Rall, 1960; Rall, 1969)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Rall's seminal work.

claim: Schierwagen devised a broader mathematical description of membrane voltage distributions in complex, highly-branched neurite trees with non-uniform boundary conditions and geometries.
source: Schierwagen then devised a broader mathematical description of membrane voltage distributions in complex, highly-branched neurite trees with non-uniform boundary conditions and geometries (Schierwagen, 1989)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Schierwagen's work.

claim: In a functioning neuron, synaptic inputs, receptors, and ion channels may shunt or amplify propagating voltage signals.
source: However, in a functioning neuron, synaptic inputs, receptors, and ion channels may shunt or amplify propagating voltage signals (London and Häusser, 2005)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to London and Häusser, 2005 and represents established knowledge in neuroscience.

claim: The transformation from neuronal morphology to electrophysiological activity patterns is often unpredictable in the absence of direct experimental assessment.
source: Thus, the transformation from neuronal morphology to electrophysiological activity patterns is often unpredictable in the absence of direct experimental assessment.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the discussion of how active properties can modify passive propagation.

claim: Measuring voltage attenuation across the many neurite paths presented in complex neuronal structures using electrophysiological techniques has proven difficult.
source: To date, measuring voltage attenuation across the many neurite paths presented in complex neuronal structures using electrophysiological techniques has proven difficult.
evidence: This claim is supported by the limited number of studies cited that have experimentally assessed electrotonus.

claim: Electrotonus has been experimentally assessed in only a handful of neuron types.
source: Thus, electrotonus has been experimentally assessed in only a handful of neuron types (for example: Spruston and Johnston, 1992; Spruston et al., 1994; Rapp et al., 1994; Carnevale et al., 1997; Stuart and Spruston, 1998; Chitwood et al., 1999; Jaffe and Carnevale, 1999; Otopalik et al., 2017b; Medan et al., 2018)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to the limited number of experimental studies on electrotonus.

claim: The 14 identified neurons of the STG present distinct, cell-type-specific electrophysiological waveforms, firing patterns and circuit functions.
source: The 14 identified neurons of the STG present distinct, cell-type-specific electrophysiological waveforms, firing patterns and circuit functions (Harris-Warrick et al., 1992)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Harris-Warrick et al., 1992.

claim: Four STG neuron types did not adhere to optimal wiring principles or Rall's 3/2 rule.
source: Interestingly, the four neuron types did not adhere to optimal wiring principles (Cuntz et al., 2010) or Rall's 3/2 rule (Rall, 1959)
evidence: This claim is supported by previous morphological characterization work cited (Otopalik et al., 2017a).

claim: STG neurons exhibit expansive neurite trees that sum to >10 mm of total cable length.
source: exhibited expansive neurite trees that sum to >10 mm of total cable length
evidence: This claim is supported by previous morphological measurements cited (Otopalik et al., 2017a).

claim: STG neurons have tortuous and long individual branches ranging between 100 µm and 1 mm in length.
source: tortuous and long individual branches (ranging between 100 µm and 1 mm in length)
evidence: This claim is supported by previous morphological measurements cited (Otopalik et al., 2017a).

claim: STG neurons have thousands of branch points with complex geometries.
source: thousands of branch points with complex geometries
evidence: This claim is supported by previous morphological measurements cited (Otopalik et al., 2017a).

claim: There was quantifiable inter-animal variability in many morphological features within STG neuron types.
source: There was quantifiable inter-animal variability in many features within neuron types
evidence: This claim is supported by previous morphological characterization work cited (Otopalik et al., 2017a).

claim: No single metric or combination of metrics distinguished the four STG neuron types morphologically.
source: no single metric or combination of metrics distinguished the four neuron types
evidence: This claim is supported by previous morphological characterization work cited (Otopalik et al., 2017a).

claim: Compact electrotonic structures may effectively counteract the potential physiological consequences of morphological variability observed in GM neurons across animals.
source: We suggested that compact electrotonic structures may effectively counteract the potential physiological consequences of morphological variability observed in GM neurons across animals (Otopalik et al., 2017a; Otopalik et al., 2017b)
evidence: This claim is a hypothesis suggested based on previous findings cited.

claim: STG neurons exhibit neurite lengths as long as 1 mm.
source: we were surprised to find that STG neurons exhibit neurite lengths as long as 1 mm
evidence: This claim is supported by previous morphological measurements cited (Otopalik et al., 2017a).

claim: STG neurons have neurite diameters between 10–20 µm at their primary neurite junctions that decrement to <1 µm at their terminating tips.
source: neurite diameters between 10–20 µm at their primary neurite junctions, that decrement to <1 µm at their terminating tips (Otopalik et al., 2017a)
evidence: This claim is supported by previous morphological measurements cited and confirmed by data in Figure 2.

claim: STG neurite geometries suggest a 1–2% taper.
source: suggesting geometries with a 1–2% taper
evidence: This claim is inferred from the diameter measurements of STG neurites.

claim: Passive cable theory suggests that voltage signals passively propagating long distances are likely to undergo a great deal of attenuation.
source: Passive cable theory suggests that voltage signals passively propagating such long distances are likely to undergo a great deal of attenuation (Rall, 1960; Rall, 1964; Rall, 1969; Jack et al., 1975; Schierwagen, 1989)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to foundational cable theory work.

claim: Experimental studies have validated predictions of cable theory in dendrites with uniform and/or smaller diameters (typically <3 µm).
source: Experimental studies to date have validated predictions presented in these theoretical studies in dendrites with uniform and/or smaller diameters (typically <3 µm; Holmes, 1989; Jaffe and Carnevale, 1999; Stuart and Spruston, 1998)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: Diameter is a critical parameter in determining electrotonic decrement in the absence of amplifying or shunting mechanisms.
source: These studies suggested that diameter is a critical parameter in determining electrotonic decrement in the absence of amplifying or shunting mechanisms.
evidence: This claim is inferred from cited experimental studies on cable theory.

claim: Previous studies did not examine electrotonus in neurites with the wide diameters exhibited by STG neurites.
source: Yet, none of these studies examined electrotonus in neurites with the wide diameters exhibited by STG neurites.
evidence: This claim is inferred from review of the cited literature on electrotonus.

claim: A library of 720 passive cable models was simulated spanning a broad range of geometries and passive properties.
source: We conducted a proof-of-concept computational characterization of electrotonus in a library of 720 passive cable models with a much broader range of geometries (Figure 1A) and passive properties (specific Ra values between 50–300 Ω x cm and specific Rm values between 1,000–20,000 Ω x cm2; see Materials and methods)
evidence: This claim is supported by the computational simulation data presented in Figure 1 and supplements.

claim: Cable models with narrow uniform diameters show voltage events that attenuate greatly with distance.
source: In this case, the voltage event attenuates greatly with distance (λeffective is approximately 300 µm).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 1B-C.

claim: For narrow uniform-diameter cables, voltage attenuation is robust and λeffective is less than 1 mm for a broad range of passive properties.
source: This voltage attenuation is robust and λeffective is less than 1 mm for a broad range of passive properties (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Cable models with STG-like geometry show smaller response amplitude at the site of activation compared to narrow uniform cables.
source: Altering the morphology of this cable model to reflect the geometry of an STG neurite (Figure 1D) results in a smaller response amplitude at the site of activation (compare maximum amplitudes in Figure 1B and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of simulation data in Figure 1B and 1D.

claim: Cable models with STG-like geometry show a robust increase in λeffective and similar signal amplitudes across the cable compared to narrow uniform cables.
source: However, this is accompanied by a robust increase in λeffective and similar signal amplitudes across the cable.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 1D-E.

claim: For STG-like cable geometries, Ra values between 50–150 Ω x cm and Rm values > 10,000 Ω x cm2 yield λeffective values greater than 1 mm.
source: Ra values between 50–150 Ω x cm and Rmvalues > 10,000 Ω x cm2 yield λeffective values greater than 1 mm.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Neurites with wide proximal diameters present relatively long λeffective values even in the presence of a large load at the proximal end of the cable.
source: Neurites with wide proximal diameters present relatively long λeffective values even in the presence of a large load at the proximal end of the cable (d0), made to mimic a putative shunt imposed by the rest of the neurite tree (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Long λeffective values can be achieved as a consequence of neurite geometry alone, in the absence of voltage-gated ion channels or other amplifying mechanisms.
source: Importantly, these simulations demonstrate that long λeffective values can be achieved as a consequence of neurite geometry alone, in the absence of voltage-gated ion channels or other amplifying mechanisms that have been implicated in boosting distally-evoked events in other neuron types (Magee and Cook, 2000; Andrasfalvy and Magee, 2001; Smith et al., 2003; Gulledge et al., 2005; Lavzin et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data and contrasted with cited studies showing active mechanisms in other neuron types.

claim: PD and LP neurons innervate two muscles in the pylorus of the foregut.
source: PD and LP neurons innervate two muscles in the pylorus of the foregut (Figure 2A)
evidence: This claim is supported by the anatomical diagram in Figure 2A.

claim: PD and LP neurons participate in the ongoing, triphasic pyloric rhythm.
source: PD and LP neurons innervate two muscles in the pylorus of the foregut (Figure 2A) and participate in the ongoing, triphasic pyloric rhythm (Figure 2B)
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 2B.

claim: PD and LP neurons can both be identified by matching their intracellular firing patterns with spiking units on the lateral ventricular nerve (lvn).
source: PD and LP can both be identified by matching their intracellular firing patterns with spiking units on the lateral ventricular nerve (lvn; Figure 2B)
evidence: This claim is supported by the electrophysiological identification method shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The VD neuron innervates the cv1 muscle of the pylorus.
source: The VD neuron innervates the cv1 muscle of the pylorus
evidence: This claim is supported by the anatomical diagram in Figure 2A.

claim: The VD neuron can be identified on the medial ventricular nerve (mvn).
source: The VD neuron innervates the cv1 muscle of the pylorus and can be identified on the medial ventricular nerve (mvn; Figure 2B)
evidence: This claim is supported by the electrophysiological identification method shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The GM neuron participates in the episodic gastric mill rhythm.
source: The GM neuron participates in the episodic gastric mill rhythm
evidence: This claim is supported by the electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The GM neuron innervates gm1, 2, and 3 muscles.
source: The GM neuron participates in the episodic gastric mill rhythm, innervates gm1, 2, and 3 muscles (Figure 2A)
evidence: This claim is supported by the anatomical diagram in Figure 2A.

claim: The GM neuron can be identified on the dorsal gastric nerve (dgn).
source: The GM neuron participates in the episodic gastric mill rhythm, innervates gm1, 2, and 3 muscles (Figure 2A), and can be identified on the dorsal gastric nerve (dgn; Figure 2B)
evidence: This claim is supported by the electrophysiological identification method shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Each STG neuron type presents highly branched and expansive neurite trees when filled with fluorescent dye.
source: When filled with fluorescent dye, each neuron presents highly branched and expansive neurite trees (Figure 2C)
evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescence images shown in Figure 2C.

claim: STG neurite paths taper from 10 to 20 µm at the soma-primary neurite junction to <2 µm at terminating tips.
source: Recapitulating previous work, we observed neurite paths that taper from 10 to 20 µm at the soma-primary neurite junction to <2 µm at terminating tips (Figure 2D–E, Figure 2—figure supplement 1–2 to Figure 2; Otopalik et al., 2017a)
evidence: This claim is supported by volumetric reconstructions shown in Figure 2D-E and supplements, and cited previous work.

claim: Geometrical taper from proximal to distal end is thought to increase the electrotonic length constant for long neurite paths.
source: Geometrical taper from proximal to distal end is thought to increase the electrotonic length constant for long neurite paths (Holmes and Rall, 1992)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Holmes and Rall, 1992.

claim: Some STG neurites tapered gradually while others presented diameters that decrease in an abrupt step.
source: Yet, we found that, while some STG neurites tapered gradually, others presented diameters that decrease in an abrupt step.
evidence: This claim is supported by morphological measurements shown in Figure 2D-E and supplements.

claim: Geometrical taper influences action potential shape and velocity.
source: Previous study has demonstrated that geometrical taper influences action potential shape and velocity (Goldstein and Rall, 1974)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Goldstein and Rall, 1974.

claim: Cables with a gradual taper presented longer λeffective than those with abrupt step reductions.
source: In brief, we found that cables with a gradual taper presented longer λeffective than those with abrupt step reductions (consistent with Holmes and Rall, 1992)
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3 and citation to Holmes and Rall, 1992.

claim: Cables with wide diameters consistent with STG neurons presented λeffective > 1 mm for even abrupt step-reductions in diameter for a range of passive properties (Ra values < 100 Ω x cm and Rm values > 10,000 Ω x cm2).
source: Yet, cables with wide diameters consistent with those measured in STG neurons (Figure 2E), presented λeffective> 1 mm for even abrupt step-reductions in diameter for a range of passive properties (Ravalues < 100 Ω x cm and Rmvalues > 10,000 Ω x cm2)
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Finer cables (tapering from 1 to 2 µm to sub-µm diameters) with any step reductions along the path of propagation resulted in λeffective < 0.5 mm.
source: This contrasts with finer cables (tapering from 1 to 2 µm to sub-µm diameters), wherein any step reductions along the path of propagation resulted in λeffective < 0.5 mm.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Synaptic sites are sparsely distributed throughout the STG neuropil.
source: Synaptic sites are sparsely distributed throughout the neuropil
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to anatomical studies (King, 1976a; King, 1976b; Kilman and Marder, 1996).

claim: Pre- and post-synaptic sites are closely apposed on the same neurites in the STG.
source: pre- and post-synaptic sites are closely apposed on the same neurites (King, 1976a; King, 1976b; Kilman and Marder, 1996)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to anatomical studies.

claim: Sufficiently large synaptic potentials may originate anywhere on the STG neurite tree, propagate in any direction, and achieve consistent neuronal output.
source: Thus, sufficiently large synaptic potentials may originate anywhere on the neurite tree, propagate in any direction, and achieve consistent neuronal output.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the compact electrotonic architecture and synaptic organization of STG neurons.

claim: The motor rhythm generated by the STG relies on slow oscillations and graded inhibitory transmission.
source: The motor rhythm generated by the STG relies on slow oscillations and graded inhibitory transmission (Eisen and Marder, 1982; Marder and Eisen, 1984; Maynard and Walton, 1975; Graubard et al., 1980; Manor et al., 1997; Manor et al., 1999; Bose et al., 2014; Golowasch et al., 2017)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to studies on STG physiology.

claim: The biophysical features described in STG neurons may allow for the averaging of very large and slow synaptic conductances in space and time, thereby sustaining pattern generation in this motor circuit.
source: The biophysical features we have described in STG neurons may allow for the averaging of very large and slow synaptic conductances in space and time, thereby sustaining pattern generation in this motor circuit.
evidence: This claim is a hypothesis inferred from the observed biophysical properties.

claim: Rhythmic networks that compute with slow oscillations and/or graded transmission may benefit from a similar biophysical and morphological architecture as STG neurons.
source: Rhythmic networks that compute with slow oscillations and/or graded transmission (Walsh et al., 1972; Wilson and Wachtel, 1974; Pearson and Fourtner, 1975; Robertson and Pearson, 1985; Angstadt and Calabrese, 1991; Dicaprio, 1989; Dicaprio et al., 1997; Dale, 1995; DiCaprio, 2003; Smarandache-Wellmann et al., 2013) may benefit from a similar biophysical and morphological architecture.
evidence: This claim is a hypothesis speculating about other neural circuits, supported by citations to examples of such circuits.

claim: Wide neurites may aid STG neurons in generating consistent physiological output in the face of variable conductance magnitudes and subcellular distributions of intrinsic and synaptic properties across animals.
source: Moreover, we suggest that wide neurites may aid STG neurons in generating consistent physiological output, in the face of variable conductance magnitudes and subcellular distributions of intrinsic and synaptic properties across animals (Prinz et al., 2004; Schulz et al., 2006; Marder and Goaillard, 2006; Goaillard et al., 2009; Marder, 2011)
evidence: This claim is a hypothesis supported by citations to studies showing variability in STG neuron properties.

claim: Spike initiation zones in STG neurons are located just outside the neuropil, where the axons exit the ganglion.
source: Moreover, spike initiations zones, where such TTX-sensitive channels are most likely to reside, are located just outside the neuropil, where the axons exit the ganglion (Raper, 1979; Miller, 1980)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to anatomical studies.

claim: PD neurons exhibit a second, dopamine-sensitive axonal spike initiation zone between the upper dvn and its split into the bilateral lvns.
source: PD neurons exhibit a second, dopamine-sensitive axonal spike initiation zone between the upper dvn and its split into the bilateral lvns (refer to Figure 2A; Bucher et al., 2003)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Bucher et al., 2003 and reference to Figure 2A.

claim: It is unlikely that TTX-sensitive voltage-gated channels would shunt the current arising from evoked events in STG neurons given the peripheral locations of the spike initiation zones.
source: Given the peripheral locations of the spike initiation zones in these neurons, it is unlikely that TTX-sensitive voltage-gated channels would shunt the current arising from these evoked events in the same way as has been seen in other systems (Laurent, 1990)
evidence: This claim is inferred from the anatomical location of spike initiation zones and contrasted with cited work in other systems.

claim: Spatial separation of spike initiation zones from synaptic integration and slow wave generation in the neuropil may reduce shunting of synaptic currents.
source: Spatial separation of spike initiation zones from synaptic integration and slow wave generation in the neuropil may reduce shunting of synaptic currents.
evidence: This claim is a hypothesis inferred from the anatomical organization of STG neurons.

claim: Given the relatively compact electrotonic architecture of STG neurons arising from their neurite geometries, other features of their morphologies and the exact spatial organization of synaptic contacts may not be critical determinants of the distinct physiological waveforms and firing patterns exhibited by different STG neuron types.
source: Taken together with previous work (Otopalik et al., 2017a; Otopalik et al., 2017b), the present study suggests that, given the relatively compact electrotonic architecture of STG neurons arising from their neurite geometries, other features of their morphologies and the exact spatial organization of synaptic contacts may not be critical determinants of the distinct physiological waveforms and firing patterns exhibited by different STG neuron types.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the findings of compact electrotonus and previous work.

claim: The different activity patterns of STG neuron types are predominantly determined by their cell-type-specific ion channel and receptor expression profiles.
source: Thus, one is left with the expectation that their different activity patterns are predominantly determined by their cell-type-specific ion channel and receptor expression profiles.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the finding that morphology alone does not distinguish neuron types.

claim: The 14 different STG neuron types express different palettes of receptors.
source: And, indeed, there is much evidence that the 14 different neuron types express different palettes of receptors (Swensen et al., 2000; Swensen and Marder, 2000; Swensen and Marder, 2001)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on receptor expression in STG neurons.

claim: The 14 different STG neuron types express cell-type-specific ratios of ion channels.
source: the 14 different neuron types express different palettes of receptors (Swensen et al., 2000; Swensen and Marder, 2000; Swensen and Marder, 2001) and cell-type-specific ratios of ion channels (Schulz et al., 2006; Schulz et al., 2007)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on ion channel expression in STG neurons.

claim: STG neurons may present expansive and complex morphologies to make appropriate synaptic contacts wherever partner neurons ramifying throughout the neuropil find each other.
source: One possibility is that this allows STG neurons to make appropriate synaptic contacts wherever partner neurons ramifying throughout the neuropil find each other.
evidence: This claim is a hypothesis speculating about the functional significance of STG neuron morphology.

claim: STG neurons likely grow to fill distinct spatial fields in the neuropil for the purpose of maximizing surface area for the reception of diffuse neuromodulatory substances.
source: Additionally, it is likely that STG neurons grow to fill distinct spatial fields in the neuropil (Otopalik et al., 2017a) for the purpose of maximizing surface area for the reception of the many diffuse neuromodulatory substances that are released in the hemolymph and by descending modulatory inputs of the stomatogastric nerve (Marder and Bucher, 2007; Blitz and Nusbaum, 2011)
evidence: This claim is a hypothesis supported by citations to work on neuromodulation in the STG.

claim: Neuromodulatory substances are released in the hemolymph and by descending modulatory inputs of the stomatogastric nerve in the STG.
source: the many diffuse neuromodulatory substances that are released in the hemolymph and by descending modulatory inputs of the stomatogastric nerve (Marder and Bucher, 2007; Blitz and Nusbaum, 2011)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on neuromodulation in the STG.

claim: For PD, LP, and GM neurons, there appears to be no substantial hyperpolarization in apparent Erevs with distance from the somatic recording site.
source: For PD, LP, and GM neurons, there appears to be no substantial hyperpolarization in apparent Erevs with distance from the somatic recording site (this is validated with linear regressions shown in Table 1)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D and statistical analysis in Table 1.

claim: GM neurons present exceptionally invariant apparent Erevs across sites on their neurite trees (mean coefficient of variance within individual GM neurons was 0.04).
source: Figure 3B shows that GM neurons present exceptionally invariant apparent Erevs across sites on their neurite trees (mean coefficient of variance (CV) within individual GM neurons was 0.04; Table 2)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D and Table 2.

claim: LP and PD neurons exhibit relatively invariant apparent Erevs (mean CVs were: 0.06, 0.05, and 0.08, respectively).
source: Likewise, LP, and PD neurons exhibit relatively invariant apparent Erevs (mean CVs were: 0.06, 0.05, and 0.08, respectively; Table 2)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Table 2.

claim: A subset of VD neurons shows higher standard deviations and CVs, suggesting heterogeneity of voltage signal propagation across the neuronal structure.
source: It should be noted that a subset of VD neurons shows higher standard deviations and CVs, suggesting heterogeneity of voltage signal propagation across the neuronal structure.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the data shown in Table 2.

claim: Statistical comparison of CVs revealed no statistically significant differences across neuron types (ANOVA, F(3, 17)=1.2 p=0.341).
source: Yet, statistical comparison of CVs (ANOVA, [F(3, 17)=1.2 p=0.341])
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claim: Statistical comparison of mean apparent Erevs revealed no statistically significant differences across neuron types (ANOVA, F(3, 17)=2.29, p=0.1154).
source: and mean apparent Erevs (ANOVA, [F(3, 17)=2.29, p=0.1154]) revealed no statistically significant differences across neuron types
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claim: The four STG neuron types are similarly electrotonically compact neuronal structures, wherein apparent Erevs typically varied by <10% of the mean within individual neurons.
source: This suggests that the four neuron types are similarly electrotonically compact neuronal structures, wherein apparent Erevs typically varied by <10% of the mean within individual neurons.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the statistical analysis and experimental data.

claim: The range of apparent Erevs translates to a range of mean apparent Erev ± 6–8 mV within each individual neuron.
source: This translates to a range of mean apparent Erev ± 6–8 mV within each individual neuron.
evidence: This claim is calculated from the experimental data on apparent Erevs.

claim: The classic cable model shows a robust inward bias in directional sensitivity of passive voltage propagation.
source: Figure 4E and F illustrate a notable difference in the directional sensitivity of passive voltage propagation in these two cable models; the classic cable model shows a robust inward bias
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The STG neurite cable model shows no directional sensitivity in passive voltage propagation.
source: the classic cable model shows a robust inward bias and the STG neurite shows no directional sensitivity
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The inward bias in the classic cable model attenuates with increasing axial resistivity (Ra) and decreasing membrane resistivity (Rm).
source: However, the inward bias in the classic cable model does attenuate with increasing axial resistivity (Ra) and decreasing membrane resistivity (Rm).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The classic cable model presents sublinear integration of inhibitory voltage events.
source: The classic cable presents sublinear integration of inhibitory voltage events.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: As the Rm decreases and Ra increases in the classic cable model, voltage summation transitions from sublinear to linear.
source: Yet, as the Rm decreases and Ra increases, voltage summation transitions from sublinear to linear.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The STG neurite cable model presents relatively linear integration across a broad range of passive properties.
source: In contrast, the STG neurite presents relatively linear integration across a broad range of passive properties.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: STG neurites will present directional insensitivity and near-linear voltage integration if they operate predominantly by passive propagation and in the absence of active properties serving to shunt or amplify voltage signals.
source: Taken together, these simulations predict that STG neurites will present directional insensitivity and near-linear voltage integration if they operate predominantly by passive propagation and in the absence of active properties serving to shunt or amplify voltage signals.
evidence: This claim is a prediction based on the simulation results.

claim: All four STG neuron types show little directional selectivity (supported by root-mean-square error values (RMSE) <0.5 mV*s).
source: Interestingly, all four neuron types show little directional selectivity (this is supported by root-mean-square error values (RMSE) <0.5 mV*s, a measure of goodness-of-fit to the identity line)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Neurites in each of the four STG neuron types do not exhibit the directional selectivity that has been described in other neuron types.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that neurites in each of these four STG neuron types do not exhibit the directional selectivity that has been described in other neuron types (Barlow and Levick, 1965; Euler et al., 2002; London and Häusser, 2005; Branco et al., 2010)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and contrasted with cited work in other neuron types.

claim: Across all STG neuron types, the majority of branches showed linear summation.
source: Across all neuron types, the majority of branches showed linear summation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: RMSE values for voltage summation were less than 1.5 mV*s across all STG neuron types.
source: RMSE values were less than 1.5 mV*s; thus, the measured response integrals were within 1.5 mV*s of the integral expected of linear summation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: GM neurons exhibited particularly uniform linear summation across all branches evaluated with a small RMSE value of 0.32 mV*s.
source: GM neurons (Figure 6Biv) exhibited particularly uniform linear summation across all branches evaluated and this is reflected in a small RMSE value of 0.32 mV*s.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6Biv.

claim: LP branches and PD branches show slightly higher RMSE values (greater than 1 mV*s), perhaps providing some evidence of variable shunting or amplifying mechanisms.
source: LP branches and PD branches show slightly higher RMSE values (greater than 1 mV*s), perhaps providing some evidence of variable shunting or amplifying mechanisms.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: RMSE values less than 2 mV*s across all cell types suggests relatively linear summation across most branches evaluated.
source: Even so, RMSE values less than 2 mV*s across all cell types suggests relatively linear summation across most branches evaluated.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data.

claim: Voltage summation arithmetic was similarly linear in the centrifugal direction.
source: Voltage summation arithmetic was similarly linear in the centrifugal direction (consult Figure 5—figure supplement 1–4 to Figure 5)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5 supplements.

claim: The photo-uncaging experiments were performed in the absence of TTX-sensitive sodium channels, which have been abolished with 10−7 M TTX in the bath.
source: It should be noted that these experiments were performed in the absence of TTX-sensitive sodium channels, which have been abolished with 10−7 M TTX in the bath.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the experimental conditions.

claim: STG neurons are built to linearly sum and unify synaptic inputs distributed across their expansive and complex structures, rather than perform distributed computations on a branch-by-branch, or subtree-by-subtree basis.
source: Taken together, these findings suggest that STG neurons are built to linearly sum and unify synaptic inputs distributed across their expansive and complex structures, rather than perform distributed computations on a branch-by-branch, or subtree-by-subtree basis.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental findings of compact electrotonus, linear integration, and directional insensitivity.

claim: This biophysical architecture in STG neurons may be achieved passively and as a simple consequence of neurite geometry.
source: Our computational simulations suggest that this biophysical architecture may be achieved passively and as a simple consequence of neurite geometry in these neurons, which present neurites with wide diameters that taper from 10 to 20 µm near the soma, to sub-micron diameters at their terminating tips.
evidence: This claim is supported by computational simulations and experimental measurements.

claim: When voltage signals propagate long distances in the absence of amplifying mechanisms, electrotonic decrement is thought to result in sublinear voltage integration and directional bias within single branches.
source: When voltage signals propagate long distances in the absence of amplifying mechanisms, electrotonic decrement is thought to result in sublinear voltage integration and directional bias within single branches (Rall, 1964; Gulledge et al., 2005; London and Häusser, 2005)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to theoretical and experimental work.

claim: Sublinear voltage integration and directional bias have been demonstrated experimentally in a variety of vertebrate neuron types in different circuit contexts, from cortex to retina.
source: This has been demonstrated experimentally in a variety of vertebrate neuron types in different circuit contexts, from cortex to retina (Barlow and Levick, 1965; Cash and Yuste, 1998; Euler et al., 2002; Poirazi et al., 2003; Polsky et al., 2004; Branco et al., 2010)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: Linear and supralinear integration are thought to require amplifying mechanisms, such as voltage-gated ion channels or distance-dependent scaling of receptors.
source: Linear and supralinear integration are thought to require amplifying mechanisms, such as voltage-gated ion channels or distance-dependent scaling of receptors (Magee and Cook, 2000; Andrasfalvy and Magee, 2001; Smith et al., 2003; Gulledge et al., 2005; Lavzin et al., 2012)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on dendritic integration.

claim: Highly-branched and expansive neuronal structures are likely to present some degree of passive voltage attenuation (in the absence of amplifying mechanisms) and perform compartmentalized computations as a consequence.
source: Collectively, these studies support the notion that highly-branched and expansive neuronal structures, are likely to present some degree of passive voltage attenuation (in the absence of amplifying mechanisms) and perform compartmentalized computations as a consequence.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the cited literature on dendritic computation.

claim: The framework for dendritic computation does not rely on the study of, or account for, the diverse dendrite and neurite morphologies observed in nature.
source: Yet, this framework for dendritic computation does not rely on the study of, or account for, the diverse dendrite and neurite morphologies observed in nature.
evidence: This claim is a critical assessment of the existing literature.

claim: The widely-accepted principles derived from the study of so-called canonical neuron types may be less general than previously thought.
source: Thus, the widely-accept principles derived from the study of so-called canonical neuron types may be less general than previously thought.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the findings that STG neurons do not follow expected patterns from canonical neuron types.
